item.title: Hip & Pelvis — Positional Release / Counterstrain
clinicalUse: Use when assessment identifies a relevant impairment in Hip & Pelvis and the parent technique fits the patient's presentation.
Primary treatment target: hip mobility, pelvic/SI-region symptoms, gait and functional loading.
Retain the technique only if it produces a meaningful within-session improvement.
patientPosition: Supine, prone or side-lying with the pelvis well supported.
Use a comfortable hip position and avoid forcing painful end range.
therapistPosition: Stand close to the pelvis/hip and use a belt when appropriate and trained.
stabilization: Stabilize pelvis when targeting the hip; stabilize the trunk/leg according to the pelvic technique.
contact: Use broad contact over proximal femur, pelvis or target soft tissue; avoid excessive pressure over groin neurovascular structures.
Locate a reproducible tender point with light palpation, then monitor it while positioning the region toward maximal comfort.
Do not maintain painful pressure on the tender point.
forceDirection: The treatment direction is indirect: shorten/unload the painful tissue until tenderness is substantially reduced, then hold without force.
dosage: Traditional teaching often uses about 90 seconds, individualized to comfort and response.
steps: 1. Record the exact comparable sign for Hip & Pelvis: hip mobility, pelvic/SI-region symptoms, gait and functional loading.
2. Screen regional red flags, contraindications and technique-specific precautions before touching the patient.
3. Position and stabilize the patient so the target is comfortable and the manual input can be localized.
4. Apply a low-force trial using the parent technique principles and the region-specific contact described above.
5. Monitor pain quality, symptom distribution, guarding and patient confidence throughout.
6. Re-test the original comparable sign immediately after the trial.
7. Keep the technique only when the response is useful, then transfer the gain into active movement, loading or self-management.
mistakes: Applying the technique because it is familiar rather than because the examination supports it.
Using more force when the response is unclear or worsening.
Failing to re-test the exact movement or function that justified the treatment.
safety: Screen fracture, severe OA irritability, postoperative restrictions, acute inflammatory pathology and red-flag pelvic symptoms.
Stop or modify if symptoms peripheralize, neurological status worsens, the response is disproportionate or the patient asks to stop.
item.visualCue: Hip & Pelvis assessment → correct regional setup → Positional Release / Counterstrain → immediate comparable-sign re-test.

subTechniques.name: Piriformis / Deep Gluteal Tender Point — Positional Release
subTechniques.target: Posterior hip deep rotator tender region
subTechniques.clinicalGoal: Reduce focal posterior-hip tenderness and guarding before mobility or strengthening.
subTechniques.patientSetup: Supine or side-lying with the hip supported. Adjust hip flexion, abduction/adduction and rotation until the tender point becomes markedly less sensitive.
subTechniques.contact: Use a comfortable monitoring contact over the posterior hip; avoid excessive deep pressure.
subTechniques.direction: Hold the position of ease without stretching the deep rotators.
subTechniques.dosage: 60–90 seconds, then return slowly to neutral.
subTechniques.reassess: Tenderness, hip rotation and sitting/walking tolerance.
subTechniques.clinicalPearl: Do not assume every posterior-hip tender point represents piriformis syndrome; use the response only as one clinical clue.
subTechniques.safetyNote: Stop if strong distal neural symptoms are reproduced.

subTechniques.name: Adductor Tender Point — Positional Release
subTechniques.clinicalGoal: Reduce adductor guarding and improve comfortable hip abduction.
subTechniques.patientSetup: Supine with the leg supported. Move the hip slightly toward adduction and flexion/rotation as needed until the point is clearly more comfortable.
subTechniques.contact: Light monitoring contact over the symptomatic adductor area while the limb is fully supported.
subTechniques.direction: Maintain the shortened/unloaded position; no stretching during the hold.
subTechniques.reassess: Adductor tenderness, hip abduction and side-step/squat tolerance.
subTechniques.clinicalPearl: The leg should feel supported enough that the patient can stop guarding.
subTechniques.safetyNote: Avoid acute adductor tear or hematoma.
